title: Data centres: A construction boom meets an infrastructure constraint
gist: Oxford Economics Australia projects data-centre construction rising from $5.3bn in FY26 to a ~$14bn peak in FY29, but power, grid and other constraints mean the announced pipeline is not a delivery forecast.

insights.claim: Data-centre construction work done is about $5.3bn in FY26 and is expected to peak near $14bn (constant 2023/24 prices) in FY29, making data centres Australia's largest non-residential building sector that year and seventh-largest construction sector overall.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Australian construction, engineering and materials demand is shifting to data centres.

insights.claim: Electricity infrastructure rises from the fourth-largest to the second-largest Australian construction sector between FY26 and FY29.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Grid build-out is a second-order beneficiary of the AI boom.

insights.claim: Broader data-centre investment including servers and land is expected to exceed $60bn annually by decade's end, but much IT equipment is imported so headline capex overstates domestic activity.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Domestic value capture is much less than headline capex.
insights.locator: Headline CAPEX is not the same

insights.claim: Data-centre electricity consumption is forecast to rise from about 5 TWh in FY26 to almost 34 TWh by FY36, lifting its share of National Electricity Market consumption from 2.8% to over 13%.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Power availability will determine project location and timing.
insights.locator: Power availability will increasingly shape where projects get built

insights.claim: Announced capacity is not realised demand: projects can be delayed, downsized or cancelled, and weaker AI returns, tighter financing or less capital-intensive computing could slow investment.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Discount announced pipelines; AI-cycle risk is a swing factor.
insights.quote: Announced capacity is not the same as realised demand.
insights.locator: Power availability will increasingly shape where projects get built

insights.claim: Data-centre clusters will also compete for water, land, specialist equipment, labour and materials, so locations with the largest announced pipelines won't necessarily see the most development.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Construction cost inflation and delays are likely where pipelines concentrate.
insights.locator: The infrastructure challenge extends beyond power

insights.claim: Buildings last decades while servers are replaced far more often, so the current cycle is construction-intensive and over time more investment shifts to technology replacement.
insights.speaker: Adric Kam
insights.so_what: Construction demand is front-loaded; long-term capex is not an equal construction pipeline.
insights.locator: Headline CAPEX is not the same
